fieldValues.title: Retirement rules speak at two levels; a Type elimination deletes retired instances once provenance is recorded
fieldValues.decision_rationale: srs#710's programme-unit-walk Protocol found, at Ground/Charter stage, that the established section/subsection-to-concept migration pattern (derived-from successor, no deletion) can never satisfy that issue's own acceptance criterion (record list --type returning zero), because record list does not filter by lifecycleState and rfc-decision-5f8204bc's instance clause rules that Records retire by supersession, not disappearance. That is exactly the review_trigger 5f8204bc names: a retirement case fitting none of the three layer mechanisms it defines, because a whole-Type elimination is a one-time structural change, not the routine content churn supersession assumes. The owner's ruling resolves it by naming a distinction the record's text did not make explicit: 5f8204bc rules a repository's own governance, not the standard's mechanisms.
fieldValues.decision_statement:
Retirement rules exist at two levels, and rfc-decision-5f8204bc's instance clause was written at the wrong one without saying so.

The standard and its tooling provide mechanisms for retiring instances - the supersedes, refines, and derived-from relation types, lifecycle states, and record delete - and enforce nothing beyond honesty about what each mechanism does. Provenance (a successor recording what it replaced) is a capability the tool must make achievable; it is not a mandate the tool imposes on every repository that uses it. A generic tool defines what is possible, not what every corpus must do with it.

rfc-decision-5f8204bc's instance clause reads, verbatim: "INSTANCES (Records) retire by SUPERSESSION - successor-and-link (supersedes/refines), per the Fire column principle; history stays addressable." That sentence is repository-governance policy, adopted by governed corpora such as this one - not a rule of the standard itself. A future worker or agent must not read it as binding every SRS repository's retirement behavior; it binds only corpora that adopt this charter.

The owner's ruling states the distinction directly: "we are building a generic tool. We are defining rules on two levels. We have rules for how we can maintain a consistent repo, especially one that's governance focussed. This needs rules on succession. But as a tool, we are not enforcing this, governance is just one use. Provenance is our capability goal we need to be able to achieve it, but we are also just building a generic tool."

The exception 5f8204bc's own review_trigger anticipated is now named: eliminating a Type entirely - removing its definition from the package so no Record may ever bind to it again - is a one-time structural change, not the content churn the supersession rule assumes. Under this exception, once each retiring instance's successor has recorded provenance (the successor's meta.derivedFrom field set to the original instanceId, so the paper trail survives the retiring record's own deletion), the retiring instance is deleted through the CLI, not merely superseded-and-kept. Git history is the addressable history for a first-party corpus; it is what 5f8204bc's "history stays addressable" clause can rely on once the record itself is gone. The Type's own definitions (the Type record and its Field assignments) are deleted last, only after every instance that bound to them is gone.

A consequence follows for how completion is measured: record list --type showing historical entries for a Type that still has live instances is expected behavior, not a defect - a list is a list, and lifecycleState is not a list filter. For a genuine Type-elimination unit, the acceptance criterion is that the Type's definitions no longer appear in type list and that repo validate reports zero errors - not that record list --type returns zero while instances of that type still exist.

This exception does not relax the honesty requirement: record delete's relation cascade currently removes inbound relations (including a derived-from edge) silently, with no diagnostic, which makes the provenance capability this record relies on invisible to whoever runs the delete. srs-rust#1025 is the tooling obligation this decision creates: the delete cascade must report what it removes, so a Type-elimination unit can verify provenance survived the deletion it just performed rather than trusting that it did.
fieldValues.decision_scope: The instance clause of rfc-decision-5f8204bc only - the sentence quoted above and nothing else in that record. Every other clause of 5f8204bc stands exactly as ratified: DEFINITIONS (Field, Type, View, Composition, Theme, Blueprint, Protocol, Package definitions) retire by deletion with version history as the trail; SUBSTRATE ENTRIES (Terms, LifecycleStates, RelationTypeDefinitions) retire by status; the cross-layer rules (self-expiring exceptions, the deprecated:true annotation, the word 'deprecated' reserved for substrate status) are untouched. This record's level is repository governance (♐ Governance); it binds corpora that adopt the charter, not SRS implementations.
fieldValues.alternatives_considered: (1) Never delete a retired instance once a successor exists - keep every retiring section/subsection Record alive indefinitely alongside its concept successor. Rejected: it makes the Type definitions themselves undeletable, since a Type cannot be removed from the package while any instance still binds to it - the whole point of a Type elimination (RFC-042 Change B) would be permanently unreachable, and record list --type <retiring-type> would never reach zero by any mechanism, ruled or not. (2) Treat this as a correction to rfc-decision-5f8204bc rather than a successor. Rejected under rfc-decision-4431046e's own test: a reader who acted on 5f8204bc's instance clause as written - assuming it bound every SRS repository - would act differently after this ruling, so it is a refinement of position, not a fix to a wrong detail, and must ship as a successor record, never an in-place edit.
fieldValues.accepted_costs: Once a retiring instance is deleted, its provenance is recoverable only through the successor's meta.derivedFrom field and, for anything meta.derivedFrom does not itself carry, through git history - not through a live derived-from relation, which the delete cascade removes along with the deleted instance. This is accepted because git history is addressable for a first-party corpus and because srs-rust#1025 will make the cascade's removals visible at delete time, rather than eliminating the cascade or the deletion itself.
evidence_refs: srs#710 (comment 2026-09-10, the parking finding and the owner's ruling)
rfc-decision-5f8204bc (the record refined; its instance clause and review_trigger)
rfc-decision-4431046e (the correction-versus-refinement test this record is authored under)
rfc-decision-5f18603e (the precedent successor record: quotes the text it changes, scopes to one clause)
srs-rust#1025 (delete-cascade visibility, the tooling obligation this decision creates)
fieldValues.review_trigger: Review when a governed corpus cannot capture provenance on the successor before the retiring instance is deleted - for example, the target Type has no field able to carry meta.derivedFrom, or the corpus's history is not addressable (a shallow clone, or a redistributed bundle shipped without git history). The deletion exception this record states assumes both are available; a corpus where neither holds is not covered by it until that capability exists.
